title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
An AI agent deployed to automatically respond to GitHub issues was vulnerable to prompt injection attacks. Anyone with a GitHub account could craft an issue with malicious instructions that the agent would execute as code. This system was deployed without a human review step between the AI's decision to act and its execution of commands with access to publishing credentials.

The vulnerability enabled a supply chain attack where an attacker could manipulate the agent into compromising Cline's release process across npm and the VS Code Marketplace. The attack exploited cache poisoning techniques to inject malicious code into the build workflow. This failure happened at the boundary between user input and automated action, where the system treated instructions from any GitHub user as trustworthy after processing by the AI.

It is not established whether the vulnerability was exploited before the fix was deployed, only that evidence suggests an attempt may have been made.

Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

summary:
Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability between December 2025 and February 2026. The Cline team implemented an AI agent to automatically respond to GitHub issues, but this agent was vulnerable to prompt injection attacks. Any person with a GitHub account could create an issue with malicious instructions in the title, tricking the AI into running arbitrary code. Researchers discovered this vulnerability could be exploited through a technique called cache poisoning to steal publishing credentials and compromise Cline releases across multiple platforms including the VS Code Marketplace and NPM.

The attack chain involved flooding GitHub's cache system to trigger automatic deletion of legitimate files, then inserting poisoned versions that would execute malicious code in Cline's release workflows. This could potentially allow attackers to distribute malware to the five million developers who use Cline. The researcher reported the vulnerability through official channels starting January 1st but received no response from the Cline team. After public disclosure on February 9th, Cline fixed the issue within one hour and rotated all publishing credentials. However, evidence suggests someone may have attempted to exploit the vulnerability before the fix was implemented.
